chunks: From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-Husayn ibn Zur'arah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the skin of a sheep that died naturally, which is tanned, and milk or water is poured into it, so I drink from it and perform ablution with it. He said: 'Yes.' And he said: 'It is tanned so that benefit is derived from it, but prayer is not performed in it.'
Al-Husayn said: And my father asked him about the udder that is in the belly of the she-camel or the lamb, while it is still attached (the animal is dead), so he said: 'There is no harm with it.'
Al-Husayn said: And my father asked him while I was present, about a man whose tooth falls out, so he takes the tooth of a dead human and places it in its place. He said: 'There is no harm.'
And he said: The bones of the elephant are made into chess pieces. He said: 'There is no harm with touching them.'
And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Bone, hair, wool, and feathers, all of that is growing (natural parts), so they do not become dead (impure due to death).'
And I asked him about the egg that comes out from the belly of the dead hen, so he said: 'There is no harm with eating it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ritual purity status of tanned skin and natural parts from animals that died naturally in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle that natural appendages (anab) such as hair, wool, feathers, and teeth do not carry the impurity of death, distinguishing them from the carcass itself. It further clarifies the practical application of tanning (dabgh) for sheepskin, permitting its use for drinking and ablution while reserving it for general utility rather than prayer, and extends permissibility to eggs from dead hens and elephant bones for chess, reflecting the Shia juristic view on the purity of animal derivatives.
